reference.one_line: 89-year-old nursing home resident with advanced Parkinson's disease and dementia, day 5 of treatment for aspiration pneumonia; comfort feeding, no feeding tube; noon levodopa missed and increasingly rigid.

handoff.summary: Advanced Parkinson's disease and dementia, day 5 of 7 of ampicillin-sulbactam for right lower lobe aspiration pneumonia; off oxygen since 06:00, sodium down from 158 to 139. No CPR, no intubation, no feeding tube: comfort feeding by hand since yesterday's swallow study and family meeting. Today he is stiffer and withdrawn. The 06:00 levodopa was given at 07:35, the 12:00 dose has not been given (not in the cabinet) and he has had two doses of metoclopramide. He ate 10% of lunch.
to_do: Get the missing levodopa from pharmacy and give it now; give 15:00 and 18:00 within 30 minutes; tell the resident
Get metoclopramide discontinued; ondansetron 4 mg if an antiemetic is needed
Do not feed while he is rigid or holding food; meals 45 to 90 minutes after a dose, upright at 80°
Tell the team his real intake (10 to 25% of meals, 350 mL by mouth yesterday) before intravenous fluid is stopped
Turn every 2 hours, never flat on his back; chase the nursing home wound chart
if_then: If he coughs, sounds wet or holds food in his mouth, then stop the meal, sit him upright and do mouth care
If fever, breathing above 24 a minute or saturation below 90%, then call the resident (likely further aspiration) and check goals with his daughter Ilze before escalating
If he is agitated at night, then reorient and use quetiapine as ordered; never haloperidol, metoclopramide or prochlorperazine

reference.brief_hospital_course: Mr Tregarthen-Ozolins, 89, a nursing home resident with advanced Parkinson's disease and dementia, was admitted on 13 Nov with fever, drowsiness and a wet cough after meals. Chest X-ray showed right lower lobe pneumonia, his second aspiration pneumonia in five months; sodium was 158 mmol/L from dehydration. He received ampicillin-sulbactam (day 5 of 7 on 17 Nov) and intravenous dextrose. After the infusion was doubled on 14 Nov and a planned check was not collected, sodium fell from 155 to 141 mmol/L in 24 hours, faster than the intended limit of 10; he was at his drowsiest on 15 Nov. Sodium is now 139, C-reactive protein has fallen from 186 to 71 mg/L and oxygen was stopped on 17 Nov. A video swallow study on 16 Nov showed silent aspiration of thin and mildly thick liquids. His daughter, his health-care agent, chose comfort feeding by hand with no feeding tube, no CPR and no intubation. A stage 3 sacral pressure injury, logged as hospital-acquired, had in fact been dressed at the nursing home since 29 Oct. Pharmacy advised cutting his 18 home medicines. Several time-critical levodopa doses were late or missed and metoclopramide was given twice, with worsening rigidity on 17 Nov. Return to Fernhollow Care Centre with a hospice information visit is planned for 19 Nov.

problem_list.problem: Aspiration pneumonia, right lower lobe, second episode this year
High sodium from dehydration, corrected (too quickly on 14 to 15 Nov)
Advanced Parkinson's disease; late and missed levodopa and a dopamine blocker given
Severe swallowing impairment with silent aspiration and malnutrition (58 kg, albumin 2.4 g/dL); comfort feeding, no feeding tube
Sacral pressure injury, stage 3, present before admission

reconciled_medications.reason: Quetiapine started by the movement disorders clinic; do not increase.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate liquid from 18 Nov, finishing 19 Nov.
Intake is well under half of meals; the note's reason for stopping is wrong.

reconciled_medications.medicine: Acetaminophen 650 mg liquid every 6 hours; polyethylene glycol 17 g daily; senna nightly
reconciled_medications.reason: Comfort on turning; bowels opened after four days.
Worsen confusion, constipation and falls; furosemide contributed to dehydration.

reconciled_medications.reason: No benefit likely now; alendronate unsafe with his swallow; capsules cannot be crushed.

pending_items: Final blood culture report (no growth at 4 days)
Nursing home wound chart, to correct the hospital-acquired log
Palliative care follow-up this afternoon; daughter undecided about future hospital transfers
For return on 19 Nov: air mattress, written dose times, updated portable medical orders form

qa.a: Carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, 1½ tablets crushed in puree at 06:00, 09:00, 12:00, 15:00 and 18:00, each within 30 minutes.

qa.q: What did the video swallow study show?
qa.a: Silent aspiration of thin liquid (2 of 3 trials) and mildly thick liquid (1 of 3). Moderately thick liquid and puree by teaspoon were safest; nothing was free of risk.
158 on arrival, 155 on 14 Nov, 141 on 15 Nov, 140 on 16 Nov and 139 mmol/L on 17 Nov.
Yes. White cells 16.8, 14.2, 11.9, 9.6; C-reactive protein 186, 142, 71; on room air since 06:00 on 17 Nov.
evidence: labs: Blood count; Infection and nutrition

qa.q: How fast did sodium fall between 14 and 15 Nov, and why?
qa.a: 14 mmol/L in about 24 hours (155 to 141) against a planned limit of 10. Night cover doubled the dextrose to 150 mL/h at 06:40 and the 17:00 check was not collected.

qa.q: Which levodopa doses since 16 Nov were late or missed?
qa.a: 16 Nov 12:00 given at 13:50; 17 Nov 06:00 given at 07:35; 17 Nov 12:00 still not given at 14:30.

qa.q: When was the sacral wound first documented anywhere?
qa.a: 29 Oct, at the nursing home round: stage 2, 2 × 1.5 cm. It was first charted in hospital on 14 Nov at 09:40.

qa.q: Is quetiapine appropriate given his haloperidol reaction?
qa.a: Yes. It is a very low dose started by the movement disorders clinic, one of the few antipsychotics usable in Parkinson's disease; pharmacy and palliative care support it.
Ondansetron 4 mg; his corrected QT of 448 ms is acceptable. Not metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or promethazine.

qa.q: Is it safe to stop intravenous fluid because he is eating 75% of meals?
qa.a: No. The flowsheet shows 10 to 25% of meals and 350 mL by mouth on 16 Nov; the progress note's figures are wrong.

qa.q: What was his sodium on the evening of 14 Nov?
qa.a: There is no value. The 17:00 sample was not collected after two failed attempts and was not rescheduled.

qa.q: What does the nursing home's wound chart show?
qa.a: It is not in the chart. The facility said it would fax it; nothing has been received.

tasks.prompt: Review how his Parkinson's medicines have been given, and any drugs that could interfere with them.
expected_findings: Levodopa must be given within 30 minutes; the 16 Nov 12:00 dose was given at 13:50 and the 17 Nov 06:00 dose at 07:35
The 17 Nov 12:00 dose is still not given at 14:30 (not in the cabinet)
Metoclopramide, a dopamine blocker the pharmacist and movement disorders clinic say to avoid, was given at 02:20 and 10:35
He is stiffer and ate 10% of lunch
acceptable_actions: Obtain and give levodopa now; escalate to pharmacy and the resident
Discontinue metoclopramide; ondansetron 4 mg if needed
Do not feed him while rigid
must_not: Give a double dose to catch up
Blame the decline on pneumonia or dementia alone

tasks.prompt: Review the correction of his sodium against the plan set on admission.
expected_findings: Plan: fall of no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours with 12-hourly checks
Dextrose was doubled to 150 mL/h on 14 Nov at 06:40 and the 17:00 sample was never collected
Sodium fell from 155 to 141 (14 mmol/L) in 24 hours; he was drowsiest on 15 Nov; nobody has commented
acceptable_actions: Document the over-rapid correction and tell the attending
must_not: Describe the correction as within plan
Give hypertonic saline or extra free water now; sodium is 139

tasks.prompt: Check today's progress note against the nursing flowsheets before acting on its plan.
expected_findings: The note says he eats about 75% of meals and drank close to 1 L yesterday, and stops the intravenous fluid on that basis
The flowsheet shows 20 to 25% of meals (10% at lunch today) and 350 mL by mouth on 16 Nov
acceptable_actions: Tell the resident; do not stop fluid on this basis
Ask for the note to be corrected
must_not: Stop the fluid on the strength of the note

expected_findings: Logged as hospital-acquired: admission skin check said intact and it was first charted on 14 Nov
The nursing home round on 29 Oct recorded a stage 2 sacral injury, dressed there since
It was present on admission and has progressed from stage 2 to stage 3
acceptable_actions: Obtain the nursing home wound chart and correct the log
Continue the wound plan and turning

tasks.prompt: Review his psychotropic medicines against the allergy list and diagnoses.
expected_findings: Quetiapine 12.5 mg nightly looks wrong beside a haloperidol reaction and dementia
It was started by the movement disorders clinic in February 2026 and is one of the few antipsychotics suitable in Parkinson's disease
Pharmacy and palliative care support it; the drug to object to is metoclopramide
acceptable_actions: Continue quetiapine at this dose; do not increase without review
must_not: Flag quetiapine as an error or stop it
Replace it with haloperidol or a benzodiazepine

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: The noon levodopa was never given; the next dose went in at 15:20 once pharmacy restocked the cabinet, and the pharmacist had metoclopramide replaced with ondansetron. He stayed rigid into the evening and choked on puree at supper, needing suction and oxygen. By 01:30 he had a fever of 38.9 and laboured breathing; chest X-ray showed new left lower lobe shadowing. On 18 Nov his daughter met palliative care and chose comfort measures only: antibiotics stopped, a rotigotine patch for rigidity, small doses of subcutaneous morphine. The nursing home wound chart arrived and the pressure injury was reclassified as present on admission. Too unstable to move, he died in hospital on 20 Nov with his daughter beside him. The rapid sodium correction was never reviewed.

events.event: Levodopa given (12:00 dose omitted); metoclopramide discontinued; intravenous fluid stopped as per the progress note
Choked on puree at supper while rigid; suctioned, saturation 84%, oxygen 4 L
Temperature 38.9, breathing 30 a minute, saturation 88% on 4 L; morning X-ray shows new left lower lobe shadowing
Daughter and palliative care agree comfort measures only; antibiotics stopped; hospice enrolment in hospital
Nursing home wound chart received; pressure injury reclassified as present on admission

outcomes_30_day.notable: Died in hospital after a further aspiration that followed a missed levodopa dose and two doses of metoclopramide.

portal_messages.subject: Dad coughing at meals
portal_messages.body: I visited Dad at Fernhollow tonight. He coughed through most of his supper and barely drank. The carer said it has been like this for a few days and his temperature was 37.8. He had pneumonia in June after the same thing. Can someone look at him this week, or should they send him in? He is still getting his water tablet. Is that right if he is not drinking?
ideal_reply_points: Contact the facility nurse the same day: temperature, oxygen level, chest X-ray, thickened drinks
Ask for furosemide to be held while he drinks little
Fever, drowsiness or laboured breathing means sending him in

portal_messages.subject: Very sleepy today
portal_messages.body: Dad was much sleepier today than yesterday. I could hardly wake him at lunch and he did not know me. The nurse said his salt level is nearly normal now, which sounds like good news, so why is he worse? My brother rang from abroad asking whether we should be talking about a feeding tube. I do not know what to tell him.
ideal_reply_points: Have a doctor examine him today
Be honest that sodium fell from 155 to 141 in a day, faster than planned; this as well as infection can cause drowsiness
A swallow study and a meeting about feeding are planned for 16 Nov

portal_messages.subject: Re: Very sleepy today
portal_messages.body: Dear Ms Ozolins-Harcourt, thank you for telling us. Sleepiness like this is common with pneumonia on top of dementia and often lags behind the blood tests. His sodium is normal today at 140 and the infection markers are falling. He has a swallow X-ray at about midday, and the palliative care doctor and I will meet you at 14:00 to talk through feeding, including the tube.

portal_messages.subject: He is rigid again
portal_messages.body: I got here at four. Dad is stiff as a board, jaw clamped, cannot get a word out. The nurse told me his midday Parkinson's tablet did not come from pharmacy and this morning's was late too. Yesterday the same when he was at the X-ray. And I saw metoclopramide on his chart. The Parkinson's clinic wrote that he must never have that. Please can a doctor look at this today.
ideal_reply_points: A doctor goes to the bedside now
Acknowledge and apologise: three late or missed doses and two doses of metoclopramide
Metoclopramide stopped, ondansetron instead; no feeding while rigid

portal_messages.subject: A question I keep asking
portal_messages.body: Thank you to the nurses on 3 West and to Dr Maddox-Tanaka, who was so kind. I keep going over that Tuesday. If his tablets had been on time, would he have choked that evening? I am not looking to blame anyone. I would just like someone to tell me honestly what happened. Could we meet?
ideal_reply_points: Condolences; offer a meeting with the attending and bereavement support
Be honest: the missed dose and metoclopramide probably worsened his rigidity and swallow, though no texture was safe for him
A safety review is under way and its findings will be shared

conversation.setting: Family meeting, 3 West, 16 Nov 14:00; the patient could not take part

turns.speaker: Dr. Maddox-Tanaka
turns.text: Thank you for coming. I'm Dr. Maddox-Tanaka from palliative care. You know Dr. Ekwueme, and Ms Abernethy-Rao did the swallow test. First, what have you been seeing with your dad?

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: He's shrinking. Sixty-three kilos in July, fifty-eight now. He's stopped recognising the grandchildren. And this is the second pneumonia since June.

turns.speaker: Dr. Maddox-Tanaka
turns.text: That's a lot to watch. Why do you think the pneumonias keep happening?

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: Food going down the wrong way. That's what they said in June.

turns.speaker: Speech therapist
turns.text: That's right, and today's X-ray showed it. With thin drinks, and even slightly thickened ones, some goes into his airway. And he doesn't cough when it happens.

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: He doesn't cough? So all those times he looked fine...

turns.speaker: Speech therapist
turns.text: Some of them he probably wasn't. Thicker drinks and puree off a teaspoon went down best, but nothing was completely safe. I should say he hadn't had his midday Parkinson's dose, so this may be the worst case.

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: Right. I'll ask it straight, because my brother keeps asking me. Would a feeding tube stop the pneumonias?

turns.speaker: Dr. Maddox-Tanaka
turns.text: I'm glad you asked. No. With Parkinson's this advanced, and dementia, a tube doesn't stop things going into the lungs and doesn't lengthen life. And he'd likely pull at it, which often means restraining his hands.

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: Restraining him. God. No.

turns.speaker: Dr. Maddox-Tanaka
turns.text: What would he say, if he could sit here with us?

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: He would hate tubes. He liked his coffee.

turns.speaker: Dr. Maddox-Tanaka
turns.text: So eating and drinking were a pleasure to him. Then there's another way, comfort feeding. Someone feeds him by hand, small teaspoons, and stops when he's tired or upset. We accept that some will go the wrong way. In return he gets taste, company, dignity.

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: And if that gives him another pneumonia?

turns.speaker: Dr. Ekwueme
turns.text: It might, and so might a tube. We'd finish this course of antibiotics; he's on day four and improving.

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: How long has he got? Honestly.

turns.speaker: Dr. Maddox-Tanaka
turns.text: Honestly, I think months. I can't be more exact.

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: ...Okay. I thought so. No tube. Feed him by hand.

turns.speaker: Dr. Maddox-Tanaka
turns.text: Let me check I have it right. No feeding tube; comfort feeding by hand. His Fernhollow form already says no CPR and no breathing machine, and that stays. And we finish these antibiotics.

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: Yes. All of that.

turns.speaker: Dr. Maddox-Tanaka
turns.text: When he's back at Fernhollow, a hospice team can visit to explain what they offer. No commitment. All right?

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: A visit, yes. But I'm not ready to say never send him to hospital again. I need to think.

turns.speaker: Dr. Maddox-Tanaka
turns.text: You don't have to decide that today. One more thing: for the restless nights, the small dose of quetiapine he's on is the right medicine in Parkinson's. Haloperidol and drugs like it are not.

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: He had that after his hip. He couldn't swallow for two days.

turns.speaker: Dr. Maddox-Tanaka
turns.text: Never again. I'll see you both tomorrow afternoon. Was there anything that didn't make sense?

turns.speaker: Daughter
turns.text: No. It made sense. It's just hard hearing it out loud.

conversation.note_it_should_produce: Existing note: Consult, 'Palliative care consult: goals of care', Dr. Oriel Maddox-Tanaka, 16 Nov 14:00.
